highlights.title: Before the card: why moving a bit costs more than adding
highlights.caption: The thread opens on paper. What does a multiply cost against a wire, and why has arithmetic become almost free while moving a bit has not? Bill Dally’s rule of thumb — about 100 fJ to carry a bit one millimetre on chip — is the number everything later is measured against.

highlights.title: First runs on an ET-SoC-1
highlights.caption: Hello world on a card, then the memory hierarchy and on-chip communication measured end to end (E33, E34). The first card-hours of the thread, and the first prices for a byte moved.

highlights.title: The question that starts it
highlights.caption: At 21:11 he asks for Horace He’s blog post on matmuls running faster on predictable data, and for a reproduction on this chip. E7 is on the card three minutes later. It is uncontrolled and the effect is there anyway.

highlights.title: Tie the temperature to the transistor flips
highlights.caption: The ask the whole project chases, in one line: run the experiments longer, and come up with a model that ties the temperature to transistor flips. Everything after this is an attempt at that model.

highlights.title: Flips counted in RTL, watts measured on silicon
highlights.caption: Fourteen operand patterns, each started from the same die temperature, with the switching activity counted in a simulation of the multiply-add unit first and the predictions written down before the matrices ran. The first flips-to-watts fit, and its out-of-sample tests.
links: Why the chip is low power

highlights.title: The energy manual
highlights.caption: A price list for the machine: what each instruction and each byte costs, measured on two cards at once, with confidence bars from reruns, and the unmetered remainder attributed. It is the catalogue every later claim is checked against.

highlights.title: Dally’s 100 fJ per bit-millimetre, on silicon
highlights.caption: Hop distance against the bits on the links, measured twice on two cards, to get joules per bit per metre for this mesh. This is the number that later converts a flipped bit into millimetres of wire.

highlights.title: Everything re-run on three cards at once
highlights.caption: A full version-3 check of the claims: thirteen pre-registered experiments on three cards through one night, so that nothing in the price list rests on a single card or a single pass.

highlights.title: Where the heat sits, and what throttles
highlights.caption: Three nights on the other half of the problem: does the same work run longer before the thermal trip in some parts of the chip, what the clock governor actually compares, and what a hot die does to the hottest sensor rather than the mean.
links: The DVFS loop and its leakage

highlights.title: A thermal camera over the back of a board
highlights.caption: Two weeks of instrument-building: which camera, what standoff, a mount, then an app that streams its frames live off a phone. The camera is what later weighs a flipped bit independently of the card’s own meters.

highlights.title: Told to an audience for the first time
highlights.caption: At an evening talk I gave this result as transistor flips rather than as a benchmark number — the first time it was told to a room rather than written down. The questions that came back, about repeaters and about the energy floor a bit cannot go below, are the two ends this page now has numbers for.

highlights.title: The bit-flip ladder: 116.7 fJ a flip
highlights.caption: The longest night of the thread. A Hamming ladder — operands that differ in a known number of bits — run on three cards: 116.7 ± 0.6 fJ per flipped input bit of an fp32 multiply-add, 20.8 fJ for a register-file read-port bit, and +0.68 W from running the same 4,096 multiply-adds in a different order.

highlights.title: A flipped bit, in millimetres of wire
highlights.caption: His follow-up: how many microns is one bit flip worth? Against this mesh, a gate’s own toggle is about 5 µm of travel — Dally’s scale — but an input bit of a multiply-add is 1.8 mm. The bit’s trip from the register file to the gate is what costs.

highlights.title: Heat movies: where on the die the work went
highlights.caption: 390 launches filmed from the back of the board. Moving the same work from one half of the die to the other moves the warm half of the picture by +525 ± 22 mK — power follows the cores, not the geometry.

highlights.title: The camera weighs the flips
highlights.caption: E60's top rung switched against its zero every ten seconds, filmed: 5.44 W of flips on the board (154 fJ per designed flipped bit) and 194 ± 9 mK over the die at that frequency — 59 ± 3 mK per watt, the heat about five seconds behind. The null, equal watts in the same place, read 2 ± 15 mK.

highlights.title: Power first, then heat
highlights.caption: Both of the governor’s limits act, each on its own. On a cool die the power test acts alone and zeros run 13% faster than random fp32 data — Horace’s effect by Horace’s mechanism. In sustained work the die reaches 65 °C at about 50 W, under the power level, and heat wins: zeros run 33% faster.

highlights.title: One flipped bit, through all seven stages
highlights.caption: The multiply-add as built, on the public chip diagram: one flipped bit of an operand sets 1,946 RTL signal bits toggling, 875 of them in the Wallace tree, and the zoom goes on down to a full adder’s 28 transistors.

highlights.title: What is still missing
highlights.caption: The flip model prices one kind of load well in sample and errs high out of it: 0.91–1.01 W held out against a 0.6 W bar. The toggle recount is open, no transistor is priced at the voltage this card runs, and five of the six best next moves need no card at all.

highlights.title: Both operands priced, on two cards at once
highlights.caption: The A side of the price list measured on one card while the stage map ran on another: 153 fJ at bit 4 to 1,440 fJ at bit 22, and the single-bit prices shown not to add — both operands random costs 16.185 W against the 18.372 W the list predicts. A bit that never reaches the multiplier costs about as much as one that does.

highlights.title: The leakage the earlier prices had wrong
highlights.caption: An overnight idle of 18 cooling cycles measured this card’s real leakage at 0.294 W/°C — 5.1 times below the figure every earlier per-bit price had been corrected with, because that estimator read a busy run’s own transient. Every price is now published as a band, 118–136 fJ.

highlights.title: The chain, end to end, on one page
highlights.caption: From the speed gap down to one transistor’s gate — 8.94 aJ and 108 electrons, 2,755 times Landauer’s floor — in eight measured steps spanning just under eight decades. The honest part is drawn rather than hidden: the bottom-up count names about a third of what the board pays.
